commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga and Samadhi
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse emphasizes that through the stabilization of the gaze (Drishti), one achieves a dissolution of the duality of objective reality (Bhuta) and sensory perception (Indriya). By retracting attention into its origin, the practitioner experiences the substratum that is beginningless and eternal.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It relates to the practice of 'Drishti Yoga' and 'Pratyahara', relevant today for psychological centering and overcoming sensory overload in an information-heavy world.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Trataka (steady gazing), Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses), Dhyana (meditation), and focus on the source of consciousness.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept addresses the Laya-avastha, where the 'vrittis' (fluctuations) of the mind cease upon focusing, leading to the identification of the 'Sanatani' (eternal, primordial nature) underlying 'Bhuta' (matter) and 'Indriya' (senses).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Provides a framework for 'mindfulness-based stillness', where detaching from external stimulation allows for mental restoration, akin to 'de-cluttering' cognitive processing to reach a baseline of psychological equilibrium.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Samadhi and Chitta-vritti-nirodha
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse serves as a philosophical inquiry into the nature of 'Laya', the state of mental absorption. It challenges the seeker to move beyond terminology and deeply investigate the phenomenological experience of consciousness merging into its source.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern spiritual practice, the term 'Laya' is often used loosely; this verse encourages a rigorous, analytical approach to meditation (Vichara) rather than accepting superficial definitions.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is Vichara (inquiry) and introspection, questioning the nature of consciousness rather than mere conceptual understanding.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept here is Laya, representing the state where Chitta-vrittis (mental modifications) cease, which is a prerequisite for Samadhi. It explores the Lakshana (definitive characteristics) distinguishing it from deep sleep (Sushupti).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to mindfulness and the dissolution of the ego-construct, where the 'I' thought is suspended to observe the silent background of awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Jivanmukti and the limitation of external scriptures
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse is a bold rhetorical device used in Advaita Vedantic or Siddha traditions to assert that mere scriptural knowledge remains external and 'public'—accessible to all but lacking the depth of direct self-realization. By comparing scriptures to a 'common woman', the author suggests that they are worldly, descriptive, and ultimately unable to grant the intimate, singular union with the Absolute (Brahman/Atman) that arises only through internal meditation.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the transition from 'Sastra-jnana' (book knowledge) to 'Anubhava' (direct experience), urging the practitioner not to become a slave to orthodox dogmas that might keep them trapped in dualistic thought patterns.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Nididhyasana (profound meditation), Viveka (discrimination), and Uparati (withdrawal from external scriptural dependence in favor of internal inquiry).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Sastra-uparati', emphasizing that 'sabda-brahman' (the scripture as sound) is distinct from 'para-brahman'. It argues that external texts are 'samanya' (common) as they provide dualistic information, whereas the realization of the self is 'visesa' (exclusive/non-dual).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This serves as a psychological warning against 'information overload' and academic intellectualism; it reminds modern seekers that reading about truth or psychology is distinct from the lived experience of mental clarity and emotional liberation.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Shambhavi Mudra / Yoga Chitta-Laya
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the physical and mental state of Shambhavi Mudra, where the practitioner balances inner awareness with a steady, unblinking gaze. By removing the habitual movement of the eyelids, the practitioner halts the fluctuations of the mind, facilitating deep meditative absorption (Chitta-Laya).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice is highly relevant in modern mindfulness and neuro-yoga, as it demonstrates the link between somatic stillness (eye movement) and psychological stability. It serves as a tool for grounding and managing high-stress states through physiological regulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice is Shambhavi Mudra, characterized by internal focus (Antarlakshya) and physical stillness of the eyes (Nimeshonmeshavarjitā).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Chitta-Laya through Prana-Laya indicates that the stabilization of the mind is intrinsically linked to the control of the vital energies (Prana), with Shambhavi Mudra acting as the bridge.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern psychology correlates this with 'interoceptive awareness' and the regulation of the autonomic nervous system. By consciously stabilizing physical markers like eye movement, one can achieve emotional self-regulation and deeper states of focused attention.

commentaries.description:
शाम्भवीमुद्रामभिनीय दर्शयति -
‘अन्तर्लक्ष्यमनन्यधीरविरतं पश्यन् मुदा संयमी

एषा स्याद्यमिनां मनोलयकरी मुक्तिप्रदा दुर्लभा ॥ १ ॥
ऊर्ध्वदृष्टिरधोदृष्टिः ऊर्ध्ववेधो ह्यधः शिराः ।

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Demonstrating the Shambhavi Mudra, [the text] says: 'The self-controlled seeker who continuously gazes at an internal focus with a single-pointed mind, and whose eyes remain free from blinking or opening, this is the Shambhavi Mudra. This secret technique was taught by Lord Shiva (Girisha) to those seeking the ultimate truth within the Tantras. For those who practice, it causes the dissolution of the mind and grants liberation, being rare and difficult to attain. Through the practice of upward-gazing, downward-gazing, or the upward piercing, one who keeps the head steady in this specific alignment becomes a Jivanmukta (liberated while alive) on this earth.'

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Samadhi and Internalization (Antarlakshya)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the necessity of silencing the dual fluctuations of the mind (chitta) and the breath (prana) by fixing them on an internal subjective reality. This internal absorption is the prerequisite for moving beyond objective awareness into the state of Samadhi.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern life, this practice acts as a bridge between high-stress external engagement and deep psychological regulation through mindfulness and breath-awareness (pranayama-laya).

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practices include Shambhavi Mudra, breath regulation, internal gazing (Antarlakshya), and steadying the vision through the balancing of Drishti (gaze) to achieve Manolaya (dissolution of mind).
commentary_faqs.answer: The primary concept is Antarlakshya (internal focus) leading to Chitta-vritti-nirodha (cessation of mental fluctuations), culminating in the Shambhavi Mudra, which unites the subjective consciousness with the absolute.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: It provides a sophisticated psychological framework for 'state-based' emotional regulation. By mechanically manipulating physical signs like blinking and gaze, one can trigger a parasympathetic nervous system response, inducing profound calmness and emotional neutrality.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Yoga-Sadhana and States of Consciousness
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the classification of advanced yogic practices (mudras) based on the practitioner's attained levels of consciousness (avastha) and the spiritual dimensions (dhama) they occupy. It posits that inner spiritual realization is not uniform but differentiated by the quality of awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the structured progression in Indian Tantric and Yogic traditions, moving from physical techniques to metaphysical states, highlighting the systematic nature of spiritual growth.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditation, Mudra, internalizing consciousness, awareness of spiritual planes.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept pertains to the classification of 'Shambhavi' and 'Khechari' as specific laya-yoga or kriya-yoga states which manifest based on 'avastha' (stages of mental evolution) and 'dhama' (ontological levels of manifestation).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this refers to the regulation of nervous system states through focused attention; it highlights that depth of experience in mental focus is correlated with the subject's baseline state of awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Dharana and Mudra (Internal Concentration)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse outlines a subtle yogic technique designed to withdraw the senses from external objects and anchor the attention upon the inner luminary principle. By stabilizing the gaze and adjusting the facial musculature, the practitioner initiates the state of Unmani—a transcendence of the restless mind.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice highlights the ancient Indian understanding of the psychophysiological link between posture (eye/brow position) and mental state, which is now recognized in biofeedback and mindfulness studies as a method to regulate the autonomic nervous system.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Trataka (steady gazing), Eyebrow center fixation (Bhrumadhya-drishti), and internal union (Samyoga).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is Unmani-mudra, a state of mind-transcendence (manonidhana) where the consciousness rests in the Jyotis (inner light) beyond the fluctuations of thought.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This acts as a physiological 'reset' switch; by manipulating the eye position, one can quieten the cerebral cortex, reducing anxiety and promoting a state of deep, calm focus.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Limitations of Scripture (Sastra-Vada)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the paradox of spiritual seekers who prioritize intellectual mastery of texts over direct experiential reality. It suggests that despite the depth of Agamas and Nigamas, one can become trapped in the conceptual 'net' of terminologies.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, this reflects the 'information overload' where people consume spiritual literature or digital content without actualizing the consciousness, remaining mere scholars rather than practitioners.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Beyond textual study, the primary practice implied is the direct experiential realization of the witness consciousness, bypassing conceptual scaffolding.
commentary_faqs.answer: The Bhashya emphasizes 'Unmani-bhava', a state where the chitta (mind) is dissolved, transcending the dualistic framework of Sastras (Agama/Nigama).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this addresses the 'intellectual bypass,' where individuals use spiritual study to avoid addressing their own mental agitation and subconscious patterns.

निस्पन्दस्य निश्चलस्य भावः निस्पन्दभावः कायेन्द्रियमनसां निश्चलत्वं तेन चन्द्रार्कौ चन्द्रसूर्यावपि लीनतां लीनस्य भावो लीनता लयः तामुपनयन् प्रापयन् कायेन्द्रियमनसां निश्चलत्वेन प्राणसञ्चारमपि स्तम्भ्यन् इत्यर्थः । तदुक्तं प्राक् - ‘मनो यत्र विलीयेत’(४.२३) इत्यादिपूर्वोक्तविशेषणसम्पन्नो योगी ज्योतीरूपं ज्योतिरिव अखिलप्रकाशकं रूपं यस्य स तथा तमशेषबीजमाकाशाद्युत्पत्तिद्वारा सर्वकारणमखिलं पूर्णं देदीप्यमानम् अतिशयेन दीप्यते इति देदीप्यमानं तं तथा स्वप्रकाशं परं कायेन्द्रियमनसां साक्षिणं तत्त्वमनारोपितं वास्तविकमित्यर्थः । तदिदमिति वक्तुमशक्यं, पद्यते गम्यते योगिभिरिति पदं परमं सर्वोत्कृष्टं वस्तु आत्मस्वरूपं एति प्राप्नोति । उन्मन्यवस्थायां स्वस्वरूपावस्थितो योगी भवतीत्यर्थः । अत्राधिकं किं वाच्यम् । अपरं वस्तु न प्राप्नोतीत्यत्र किं वक्तव्यमित्यर्थः ॥ ४१ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: In the Vasistha context: At the distance of twelve finger-widths, at the tip of the nose, in the pure space; the state of one who is motionless is the state of stillness, meaning the immobility of body, senses, and mind. By that, even the Moon and Sun (the Ida and Pingala nadis) merge into dissolution. By thus attaining the stillness of body, senses, and mind, one restrains even the flow of Prana. As stated earlier, 'Where the mind dissolves...' such a yogi, endowed with these characteristics, realizes the luminous form which is the source of all (Akasha, etc.), the cause of everything, full and resplendent. That supreme Reality, the witness of body, senses, and mind, which cannot be expressed as 'this is that', is the supreme abode attained by yogis. The meaning is that in the state of Unmani, the yogi remains established in their own essential nature.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: वसिष्ठ मुनि के अनुसार: बारह अंगुल के विस्तार में, नासिका के अग्र भाग में, निर्मल आकाश में; जो स्पंदन रहित है, उसका भाव ही निस्पन्द भाव है, जिसका अर्थ है काया, इन्द्रियों और मन का निश्चल होना। इससे चन्द्र और सूर्य (इडा और पिंगला) भी लय हो जाते हैं। काया, इन्द्रिय और मन के इस निश्चलत्व से प्राण का संचार भी स्तम्भित हो जाता है। पूर्वोक्त विशेषताओं से युक्त योगी उस ज्योति स्वरूप को प्राप्त करता है जो समस्त आकाश आदि का कारण है, पूर्ण है और देदीप्यमान है। वह परम तत्त्व जो काया, इन्द्रियों और मन का साक्षी है, जिसे 'यह' कहकर व्यक्त नहीं किया जा सकता, वही परम पद है जिसे योगी प्राप्त करते हैं। तात्पर्य यह है कि उन्मन्यावस्था में योगी अपने स्वरूप में अवस्थित हो जाता है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Dhyana-Yoga (Meditative Absorption)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the physical and mental posture essential for concentration (Ekagrata). By restricting the sensory intake through half-closed eyes and focusing the gaze, the yogi facilitates the withdrawal of the mind from external objects towards the internal Self.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These techniques are the precursor to modern mindfulness practices, emphasizing the somatic connection between physical stillness and the stabilization of cognitive processes, relevant for reducing anxiety and mental fragmentation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practices prescribed include 'Nasagra-drsti' (gaze at nose tip), 'Prana-stambhana' (cessation of breath-flow), and 'Indriya-nigraha' (restraint of senses).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on 'Unmani-avastha' (the state beyond the mind) and 'Laya-yoga', where the dissolution of the 'Candra-Surya' (Ida-Pingala) currents leads to the stillness of the 'Antahkarana'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the transition from a distracted state to a flow state or deep meditative concentration, illustrating how physiological regulation (gaze/posture) directly influences neurological stability and emotional regulation.

sanskrit_shloka: दिवा न पूजयेल्लिङ्गं रात्रौ चैव न पूजयेत् ।
text: दिवा न पूजयेल्लिङ्गं रात्रौ चैव न पूजयेत् ।
transliteration: divā na pūjayelliṅgaṃ rātrau caiva na pūjayet.
translation: One should not worship the Linga (the mark of the Self) during the day, nor should one worship it during the night.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
उन्मनीभावनायाः कालनियमाभवमाह -
‘ध्यानोपहार एवात्मा ध्यानमस्य माहार्चनम् ।
रात्रौ चन्द्रसञ्चारे च नैव पूजयेत् नैव भावयेत् । चन्द्रसूर्यसञ्चारे चित्तस्थैर्याभावात् । ‘चले वाते चलं चितम्’ इत्युक्तत्वात् । दिवारात्रिनिरोधतः सूर्यचन्द्रौ निरुध्य । ल्यब्लोपे पञ्चमी । तस्याः तसिल् । सर्वदा सर्वस्मिन् काले लिङ्गम् आत्मानां पूजयेत् भावयेत् । सूर्यचन्द्रयोः निरोधे कृते सुषुम्नान्तर्गते प्राणे मनःस्थैर्यात् । तदुक्तम् - ‘सुषुम्नान्तर्गते वायौ मनः स्थैर्यं प्रजायते । ’ इति ॥ ४२ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Explaining the absence of temporal rules for the state of 'Unmani' (the state beyond the mind): 'The Atman itself is the offering of meditation, and meditation is the supreme worship of Him.' One should not worship or contemplate during the day or night (specifically when the moon and sun energy circulate). Why? Because when the sun (Pingala) and moon (Ida) are active, the mind lacks stability. As it is said, 'When the breath (Vayu) moves, the mind moves.' By stopping the day and night (the breath), and checking the sun and moon channels, one should always, at all times, worship and contemplate the Linga (the Self). When the sun and moon are checked, the Prana enters the Sushumna, and thus stability of the mind is attained. It is said, 'When the breath enters the Sushumna, stability of the mind is produced.'

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: उन्मनी अवस्था के लिए काल-नियमों के अभाव को स्पष्ट करते हुए कहते हैं- 'ध्यान ही अर्पण (उपहार) है और ध्यान ही सर्वोच्च पूजन है।' दिन में या रात में जब सूर्य और चंद्र का संचार होता है, तब पूजन या भावना नहीं करनी चाहिए। क्योंकि सूर्य और चंद्र के संचार में चित्त में स्थिरता नहीं होती। जैसा कहा गया है- 'जब श्वास चलता है, तो चित्त चंचल होता है।' दिन-रात्रि (श्वास) का निरोध करके, सूर्य और चंद्र को रोककर, सदा सर्वदा लिंग (आत्मा) की पूजा करनी चाहिए। सूर्य और चंद्र के निरोध होने पर प्राण सुषुम्ना में प्रविष्ट होता है, जिससे मन में स्थिरता आती है। यही कहा गया है- 'सुषुम्ना में वायु जाने पर मन की स्थिरता उत्पन्न होती है।'

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Atma-Puja (Worship of the Self) beyond time duality.
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse transcends conventional ritualistic worship by suggesting that true devotion to the Atman is not bound by the limitations of day or night. It emphasizes that constant internal communion supersedes temporal duality, pointing toward the state of constant awareness (Unmani).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This reflects the Advaita Vedanta perspective where external ritual is a stage toward inner realization, suggesting that the practitioner should aim for a state of continuous mindfulness that persists through all circadian rhythms.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama (breath regulation), Nadi-nirodha (stopping the movement of solar/lunar channels), and internal meditative absorption.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on Unmani-bhava, where the Duality of Ida (Chandra) and Pingala (Surya) is transcended through the Nadi-nirodha (cessation of breath), leading to the realization of the Atma-linga.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to achieving a flow state or deep meditative stability, where the 'mental fluctuation' induced by external sensory stimulation (rhythms of energy) is harmonized to achieve profound psychological presence.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga / Prana Samyama
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the yogic process of internalizing the wandering prana (breath) into the central channel (Sushumna), referred to here as the 'void'. By balancing the lunar (Ida) and solar (Pingala) currents, the practitioner enters a state of non-dual stillness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient somatic understanding of the body as a network of energy channels, emphasizing that internal stillness is achieved through the regulation of breath rather than external intellectual pursuit.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Kumbhaka, and Laya (dissolution of consciousness into the central channel).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Shunya' represents the central channel (Sushumna) or the state of 'Chittavrittinirodha' where the duality of Prana and Apana is transcended.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This mirrors modern psychological concepts of 'flow state' and autonomic nervous system regulation through rhythmic breathing, which reduces cortisol and stabilizes emotional volatility.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga and Samadhi
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the internal physiological and meditative state where the practitioner equilibrates the solar (Pingala) and lunar (Ida) energy channels. By resting in the central void (Sushumna nadi), the practitioner achieves a state of non-dual stillness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It reflects the ancient Indian understanding of subtle physiology, where the goal is to transcend external sensory perception and internal mental fluctuations to rest in pure awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditation on the central channel (madhya-mārga), breath retention (kumbhaka), and sustained focus on the point of equilibrium between binary forces.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Nirālambāntara refers to the 'sunya' or void within the central channel, representing the state of Śūnyatā or Advaita where the duality of Sun (energy) and Moon (mind) vanishes.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern context, this equates to mindfulness and 'the power of now,' providing a psychological framework to achieve emotional regulation by centering oneself away from the dualistic pulls of desire and aversion.

sanskrit_shloka: सोमाद् यत्रोदिता धारा साक्षात् सा शिववल्लभा ।
text: सोमाद् यत्रोदिता धारा साक्षात् सा शिववल्लभा ।
transliteration: somād yatroditā dhārā sākṣāt sā śivavallabhā.
translation: Where the flow (of nectar/consciousness) arises from the Soma (the moon-center or the thousand-petaled lotus), that very stream is directly the beloved of Shiva (the supreme energy or Shakti).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Kundalini Yoga / Tantric Physiology
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the movement of conscious energy (Shakti) originating from the higher energy center (Soma-cakra) in the subtle body. It identifies this flow of consciousness as the divine feminine energy that is inseparable from the supreme consciousness (Shiva).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the context of Samadhi-nirupana, it emphasizes the experiential realization of energy flow in meditation. It underscores the Vedic and Tantric view that the internal experience of bliss is a manifestation of the divine union between Shiva and Shakti.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditation on the crown center (Brahmarandhra), observing the subtle 'Spanda' or internal flow of energy, and the cultivation of the union between awareness (Shiva) and energy (Shakti).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on the 'Soma-dhara', the descending nectar representing the manifestation of 'Shakti' from 'Soma' (the crown center), equating it to the primordial 'Shiva-vallabha'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Reflects the psychological state of 'flow' or peak consciousness, where the individual experiences a surge of inspiration or clarity (the stream) as a direct connection to a higher, universal self-awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga / Khechari Mudra
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse refers to a specific technique in Hatha Yoga where the tongue is inserted into the nasopharynx to redirect subtle energies. By filling the space at the back of the palate, the practitioner locks the 'amrita' (nectar) and stabilizes the mind in the 'khechari' state.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the psychosomatic connection where physical control of the tongue and breath influences consciousness, a practice still central to traditional yogic discipline for transcending ordinary perception.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Jihva-sanchalana (tongue manipulation), Nabho-mudra, and the specific practice of filling the palate (talumula) with the tongue to stabilize the prana.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Khechari relates to 'kham carati iti khechari', implying the movement of consciousness in the 'kha' (akasha/space) of the head. It facilitates the state of Umani or Turyavastha.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a secular context, this mirrors the vagus nerve stimulation techniques that help regulate the parasympathetic nervous system, promoting deep states of relaxation and emotional regulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga (Dissolution of Mind)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the practice of focusing awareness on the 'Ajna Chakra' (the point between the eyebrows). By centering consciousness in this 'Shiva-sthāna', the agitated fluctuations of the mind cease, leading to a state of meditative absorption.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient Indian psychological focus on concentration techniques. In modern times, it relates to mindfulness and the physiological benefits of focused gaze (Trataka) to reduce stress and cognitive load.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Dhāraṇā (focused concentration) upon the bhrūmadhya (eyebrow center) leading to dhyāna and eventually samādhi.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Ajna Chakra' as the 'Śivasthāna', representing the point of transcendence where individual 'manas' merges with the universal consciousness, leading to 'layāvasthā' or the state of dissolution.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Practically, this is a profound method for sensory regulation. By disengaging from external visual stimuli and focusing the internal 'gaze', one can achieve emotional equilibrium and deep psychological relaxation, serving as a neuro-biological 'off-switch' for over-stimulation.

sanskrit_shloka: अभ्यसेत् खेचरीं तावत् यावत् स्यात् योगनिद्रितः ।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga and Samadhi
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes sustained effort in Hatha Yoga practices until the practitioner transcends ordinary waking consciousness. It suggests that external practice is a preparatory necessity for internal absorption in the state of Yogic slumber, where the mind ceases its modifications.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This reflects the traditional pedagogical approach in Indian spiritual systems: intensive discipline is required to achieve spontaneous meditative states, ensuring that practice is not merely mechanical but transformative.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Constant repetition (abhyasa) of the yogic technique (khechari) until the spontaneous state of internalized consciousness (yoganidrita) occurs.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'Khechari Mudra' leading to 'Yoganidra', a state of 'samadhi' where the 'chitta' (consciousness) merges into the 'akasha' (void/ether).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern psychological context, this relates to the 'flow state' and the biological transition into parasympathetic dominance, moving from active cognitive effort to a profound state of restful awareness and mental integration.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Samadhi and Chitta-vritti-nirodha
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse prescribes a state of profound mental suspension where the mind ceases to grasp at external objects or internal concepts. By removing all 'alambana' (support or content), the consciousness enters a state of 'Nirvikalpa' or objectless awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice is central to Raja Yoga and Advaita Vedanta as a method to achieve deep meditative absorption, stripping away the mental constructs that veil the pure self.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The prescribed practice is 'Pratyahara' (withdrawal of senses) followed by 'Nischintata' (the act of not thinking), which facilitates the cessation of the mind's habitual projection.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Niralamba-Samadhi', the state where the 'Chitta' is devoid of 'Vishayas' (objects) or 'Vritti' (modifications), leading to pure 'Chaitanya'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern psychological terms, this serves as a technique for 'cognitive de-identification' or 'mindfulness-based de-construction', helping individuals detach from anxious thought-loops and achieve baseline mental stability.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga and Breath Control (Pranayama)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the process of absorption where the practitioner transcends the distinction between internal and external breath. By merging the vital energy into the central channel (madhya), the fluctuations of the mind cease.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the experiential nature of meditation, moving beyond theoretical knowledge to the direct dissolution of the subject-object duality.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Dharana, Laya-yoga, and steady introspection into the stillness of the middle path.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around Laya-samadhi, where vāyu (prāṇa) undergoes laya (dissolution) into the madhya (sushumna nadi or the core of consciousness), leading to the transcendence of the duality of bahya (external) and madhya (internal).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a psychological sense, it represents the technique of 'de-centering'—learning to let go of external environmental stimuli to find a 'middle' state of emotional equilibrium and mental clarity, providing a tool for stress management and cognitive detachment.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: एवमुक्तप्रकारेण वायुमार्गे प्राणमार्गे सुषुम्नायामित्यर्थः । दिवानिशं रात्रिन्दिवम् अभ्यस्यतः अभ्यासं कुर्वतः योगिनः अभ्यासात् यत्र यस्मिन्नाधारे वायुः प्राणो जीर्यति क्षीयते लीयत इत्यर्थः । तत्रैव वायोः लयाधिष्ठाने मनः चित्तं लीयते जीर्यत इत्यर्थः ॥ ५२ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: In this way, the 'path of the air' refers to the 'path of the Prana', meaning the Sushumna-nadi. 'Day and night' refers to 'all the time'. For the Yogi who is practicing, the place where the Vayu (Prana) becomes withered, exhausted, or absorbed—at that very locus of the dissolution of breath, the Manas (mind/consciousness) also becomes absorbed and withered.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Chitta-Laya (Dissolution of Mind)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes the necessity of constant, rigorous practice (Abhyasa) within the subtle energy channels. By focusing the life force (Vayu) systematically, the practitioner facilitates the natural dissolution of the flickering mind into the source.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, this relates to mindfulness and breath-work techniques, suggesting that cognitive calmness is achieved not by fighting thoughts, but by stabilizing the underlying biological and energetic rhythm.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Constant (divanisham) regulation of breath (vayu-margabhyasa) to induce mental stillness.
commentary_faqs.answer: Prana-laya as the primary condition for Chitta-laya within the Sushumna-nadi context.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychosomatic regulation: The link between respiratory stability and emotional equilibrium, mirroring modern biofeedback and vagus nerve stimulation theories.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse refers to the meditative practice of visualizing the descent of divine cooling energy or nectar, often associated with the cooling effect of Chandra-nadi or Kundalini-shakti within the subtle body. It emphasizes the total purification of the physical sheath (Annamaya Kosha) through meditative immersion in refined, spiritualized consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient Indian concept of 'Soma' or 'Amrita' not merely as a mythological substance, but as a psychological and physiological state achieved through deep relaxation and concentration techniques used in yoga and meditation traditions.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Visualization, Dhyana, Pratyahara, and Nadi-shodhana are the prescribed practices to invoke this internal experience.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is Amrita-plavana, a meditative visualization (dhyana) where the practitioner experiences the inner nectar (amrita-srava) bathing the entire physical frame, signifying the union of Prana and Mana.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents advanced techniques of 'somatic experiencing' or guided imagery, used in modern secular mindfulness to reduce cortisol levels, induce deep physiological calm, and mitigate psychosomatic stress.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga / Tantric Meditation
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the non-dualistic integration of awareness (manas) and primal kinetic energy (shakti). By dissolving the mental construct into the energy field and vice versa, the duality between subject and object is neutralized.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient understanding of bio-energetic consciousness, which remains relevant today as a template for mindfulness-based practices that focus on the 'internal centering' of the practitioner's psychological awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pratyahara (withdrawal), Dharana (concentration), and Laya (dissolution of mental activity into the source).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Shakti-Manas Samayoga' (union of mind and primal energy), emphasizing the dissolution of Vikalpa (mental construct) into the Spanda (vibration) of Shakti.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In contemporary psychological terms, this is a method of 'Self-Regulation' and 'Cognitive Integration,' where internal physiological arousal (Shakti) and mental cognition (Manas) are synchronized to achieve a state of flow or peak performance.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Advaita / Dhyana-Yoga
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse instructs the practitioner to achieve a state of non-dual consciousness where the internal self (Atman) and the external vastness (Akasha) are perceived as non-distinct. By dissolving the boundary between the inner subject and the outer objective reality, one attains the state of Samadhi.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It reflects the Upanishadic teaching that the microcosm is identical to the macrocosm, a foundational principle for meditation practices aiming to transcend narrow individual ego-boundaries.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is a form of meditative visualization (Dharana) where the practitioner consciously expands the sense of self to encompass the void and contracts the cosmic void to reside within the heart-center.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on the identification of the Antaratman (inner self) with the Mahakasha (great space), essentially practicing the Advaitic dissolution of the Dvaita (duality) of subject and object.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the integration of ego-boundaries; it functions as a mindfulness technique to alleviate existential anxiety by shifting focus from the 'limited individual' to an 'expansive, non-attached awareness' akin to the vastness of space.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Advaita Vedanta (Non-duality) and Samadhi
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse employs the analogy of a pot in space to describe the enlightened consciousness. Just as the space inside a pot is identical to the space outside when the pot is broken (or is always the same space), the consciousness of the sage is free from the limitations of the body and the world.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This illustrates the psychological state of 'non-attachment,' where an individual remains unaffected by external circumstances, viewing the world as a transient manifestation within the infinite consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice is 'Samadhi' and 'Sakshi-bhava' (the attitude of the witness), detaching consciousness from internal mental projections and external physical realities.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Akasha-drishthanta' or the metaphor of space, illustrating 'Atman' as 'Asanga' (unattached) and 'Shunya' (void of egoic limitation/qualities).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern context, this relates to mindfulness and cognitive detachment, helping individuals reduce anxiety by recognizing that the 'self' is not defined by external achievements or internal stress, but remains a steady, open space of awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Nirvikalpa Samadhi / Mental Stillness
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse prescribes a state of transcendence where the practitioner must go beyond both the distractions of the material world and the subtle preoccupations of the mind. By abandoning both external engagement and internal rumination, the seeker attains a state of pure consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This is crucial in the context of Samadhi, where the goal is to silence the mind entirely rather than shifting focus from one object to another.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice is 'Manolaya' (dissolution of the mind) or 'Nirvikalpa' (non-conceptual state) by refraining from any form of discursive thought.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept addresses 'Cittavritti-nirodha' (cessation of mental fluctuations), advocating for the avoidance of both 'Bahya-vishaya' (external objects) and 'Antara-kalpana' (internal conceptualization) to achieve 'Akhanda-chaitanya'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern psychology, this correlates with 'Mindfulness' and 'De-identification' with thought streams, offering a secular path to reducing anxiety caused by excessive rumination (overthinking) about external stressors and internal ego-narratives.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Drishṭi-Sṛiṣṭi-Vāda (Creation through Perception)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse posits that the objective world possesses no independent existence outside of the consciousness that perceives it. Reality is a manifestation of mental constructs, meaning that changing the mental projection directly alters the experience of the world.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It challenges the materialistic assumption of a stable, independent external reality, encouraging individuals to take radical responsibility for their subjective experience in modern life.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is 'Chinta-parityaga' (abandonment of preoccupations) and 'Manonasha' (dissolution of the mind) to achieve 'Shanti' (peace).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept here is 'Sankalpa-Kalana', where the external world (Jagat) is essentially 'Chitta-spanda' or mental vibration, aligning with the Advaita Vedanta view of 'Ajatavada'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This mirrors cognitive psychological perspectives where one's internal framing (schemas) determines their reality; by managing mental constructs, one achieves emotional regulation and existential tranquility.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya (Dissolution/Merging)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse illustrates the process of Samadhi through metaphors of total dissolution. It posits that when the finite ego interacts with the infinite essence, the individuality is surrendered, resulting in non-dual unity where the object of perception and the subject become indistinguishable.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These metaphors serve as foundational pedagogical tools in Vedantic and Yogic traditions to explain 'Atma-Brahma-Aikya' (the oneness of self and Absolute). They emphasize that spiritual realization is not a process of addition, but one of shedding superficial identities to reveal the underlying truth.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is dhyana (meditation) leading to samadhi, characterized by the intentional cultivation of non-attachment and the meditative focus required to reach the state of merging.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Laya refers to the disappearance of the ahamkara (ego) within the Brahman, where individual identity becomes indistinguishable, similar to the way physical matter loses its distinct form within its source elements.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the concept of 'flow state' and the dissolution of the self-referential ego, which is essential for emotional regulation, reducing existential anxiety, and achieving peak mental performance by eliminating cognitive distraction.

translation: All that is to be known, all that is perceived, and even knowledge itself—all this is termed the Mind.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: मनसो विलये जाते द्वैतमपि लीयत इत्याह त्रिभिः - ज्ञेयमिति । सर्वं ज्ञेयं ज्ञानार्हं प्रतीतं च ज्ञातं च ज्ञानं च इदं सर्वं मन उच्यते । सर्वस्य मनःकल्पनामात्रात्वात् मनःशब्देन उच्यते । ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं च समं मनसो विलये मनसा सार्धं नष्टं यदि, तर्हि द्वितीयकः द्वितीय एव द्वितीयकः, पन्थाः मनोविषये नास्ति । द्वैतं नास्तीति फलितार्थः ॥ ६० ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: By saying 'Jñeyam...', the author explains that when the mind dissolves, duality also dissolves. All that is to be known (jñeyam), all that is perceived (pratītam), and knowledge itself (jñānam)—all this is termed 'Mind.' Because everything is merely a projection of the mind, it is spoken of as 'Mind.' If the knowledge and the known dissolve simultaneously along with the mind, then no secondary entity remains; the path of duality does not exist in the domain of the Mind. The result is that duality does not exist.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: ‘ज्ञेयमिति’ इस प्रकार कहकर (लेखक) यह बताते हैं कि मन का विलय होने पर द्वैत भी विलीन हो जाता है। जो कुछ जानने योग्य है, जो प्रतीत है, और स्वयं ज्ञान है—यह सब मन ही कहा जाता है। क्योंकि सब कुछ मन की ही कल्पना मात्र है, इसलिए इसे मन शब्द से कहा जाता है। यदि ज्ञान और ज्ञेय मन के विलय के साथ ही नष्ट हो जाते हैं, तब दूसरा कोई (द्वितीयक) नहीं बचता; मन के विषय में (द्वैत का) कोई मार्ग नहीं है। निष्कर्ष यह है कि द्वैत का अस्तित्व नहीं है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Manodvaita / Cittasya Kalpanā
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse posits that the entire structure of subject-object duality (knower, known, and knowledge) is a projection of the Mind. When the mind ceases its conceptual activity, this duality collapses into the non-dual consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes that reality is not external but a mental construction, urging one to move beyond intellectual constructs to understand the nature of the Self.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is Manolaya or the stillness of the mind (citta-vṛtti-nirodha), where one observes the dissolution of mental projections.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept addresses the resolution of triputi (knower, known, knowledge) into the singular substratum of Manas which itself eventually dissolves into the Atman, achieving Advaita (non-duality).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to the constructivist view of reality, suggesting that our cognitive filters create our subjective world. Recognizing this 'mental construction' helps in detachment from stressors and mental anxieties.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Drishya-Viveka (Discrimination between Seer and Seen)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse asserts the Advaita Vedanta position that the objective universe is an appearance projected onto consciousness. By defining the world as 'mind-perceived,' it reduces the ontological status of the world to mental manifestation rather than independent reality.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This provides a foundation for psychological detachment, teaching individuals that external conflicts or dualities arise from mental interpretation, thus serving as a tool for managing mental stress and ego-based reactions.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Manonāśa (dissolution of the mind) and Dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda (the theory that perception is creation).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Manodṛśyam suggests that the Jagat (world) lacks Svatantra-sattā (independent reality) and is a Vivarta (superimposition) on the pure Cit (consciousness).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: It mirrors constructivist psychology, acknowledging that our experience of reality is filtered through mental constructs and cognitive biases rather than being a direct reflection of an objective 'out there' world.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Manolaya (Dissolution of the Mind)
commentary_faqs.answer: The mind is defined by its movement toward external objects (jñeyavastu). When this external orientation is withdrawn, the mind ceases to function as a separate entity and subsides into the underlying consciousness (Atman).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This is a foundational principle in Advaita Vedanta and Yoga philosophy, emphasizing that peace is not achieved by engaging the world but by settling the fluctuations of consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses), Vairagya (dispassion), and Dhyana (meditation) are the implied practices to facilitate this mental dissolution.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Manolaya involves the cessation of the vrittis of the antahkarana by removing the focus from vishaya (objects), leading to the recognition of svaprakasha consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern psychological context, this equates to 'de-identification' from external stimuli and sensory overload, serving as a template for mindfulness and stress-reduction techniques.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Anubhava (Direct Realization)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that theoretical knowledge of spiritual methods is insufficient unless validated by personal realization. True understanding in the path of Samadhi requires the integration of objective instructions with subjective, lived experience.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This highlights the 'scientific' approach in Indian philosophy where truth is not merely dogmatic but experiential, making it highly applicable to modern psychology and mindfulness practices.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditative introspection, Samadhi-abhyasa, and self-validation of teachings through cognitive-affective experience.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on Anubhava, where Jnana (knowledge) matures into realization. It suggests that Upayas (methodologies) remain intellectual constructs unless they are Anvitah (infused/connected) with the practitioner's inner state.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern psychological models of 'embodied cognition' reflect this verse, noting that transformative learning occurs only when abstract information is integrated into the individual's experiential framework.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: सुषुम्नादिभ्यः कृतकृत्याः ताः प्रणमति - सुषुम्नायै इति । सुषुम्ना मध्यनाडी तस्यै कुण्डलिन्यै आधारशक्त्यै चन्द्रात् भ्रूमध्यात् जन्म यस्याः तस्यै सुधायै पीयूषाय मनोन्मन्यै तुर्यावस्थायै चित् चैतन्यात्मा स्वरूपं यस्याः सा तथा तस्यै, महती जडानां कायेन्द्रियमनसां चैतन्यसंपादकत्वात् सर्वोत्तमा या शक्तिः चिच्छक्तिः पुरुषरूपा तस्यै । तुभ्यमिति प्रत्येकं सम्बध्यते । नमः प्रह्वीभावोऽस्तु ॥ ६४ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: The author bows to those who have achieved the ultimate goal through the Sushumna, etc. 'Sushumna' is the central channel; to that, to the Kundalini (the base power), to the one whose birth is from the moon (the eyebrow center), to the Sudha (the nectar), and to the Chit (pure consciousness) which is the very nature of existence. The power which is supreme because it imparts consciousness to inert physical bodies, senses, and minds, and is the Chit-shakti—to that power, salutations. 'Namah' (salutation) should be connected with each name. Salutations mean the act of bowing down in humility.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: सुषुम्ना आदि के द्वारा जो कृतकृत्य हो गए हैं, उन्हें प्रणाम करते हैं - 'सुषुम्नायै' इत्यादि। सुषुम्ना मध्य नाड़ी है, उसी को कुण्डलिनी (आधार शक्ति) कहते हैं। चन्द्र (भ्रूमध्य) से जिसका जन्म है, उस सुधा (पीयूष) को, जो मनोन्मनी और तुर्यावस्था है। जो जड कायेन्द्रिय-मन को चैतन्य प्रदान करने वाली सर्वोच्च शक्ति चित्-शक्ति है, उस पुरुषरूपा को नमन है। 'तुभ्यम्' का प्रत्येक के साथ सम्बन्ध है। नमः का अर्थ प्रह्वीभाव (झुकना/विनम्रता) है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Kundalini Yoga and Subtle Body Physiology
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse outlines the anatomical and energetic components of the subtle body, focusing on the activation of the Sushumna channel and the rise of the Kundalini. It highlights the transformation of consciousness through the experience of the lunar nectar (amrita) within the system.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These concepts are foundational to Hathayoga and Tantric practices, emphasizing the human body as a sacred laboratory for spiritual realization rather than merely a physical vessel.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice involves the meditation on the subtle Nadi system, awakening the Kundalini, and achieving the state of Manonmani (transcendental mind) through the circulation of inner nectar.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around Chit-shakti (consciousness power) operating through the Nadi-system, specifically Sushumna, facilitating the flow of nectar (Amrita/Sudha) which originates from the Bindu/Moon center (Chandra-janman).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the transition from cognitive, sense-bound perception to a state of internal flow (autotelic state), where physiological 'inertia' is replaced by high-awareness consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Upaya (Methodology for Enlightenment)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse addresses the inclusivity of spiritual practice, affirming that profound realization is not reserved solely for the intellectually gifted. It validates simplified methods for those who struggle with complex metaphysical conceptualization.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This reinforces the pragmatic Indian tradition of 'Yogyata-anurup-upaya' (method according to capability), ensuring that spiritual growth remains a universal possibility regardless of one's initial intellectual acumen.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Nadanusandhana (Laya Yoga practice focusing on inner cosmic resonance).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around 'Upaya-kaushalya' (skill in means), specifically identifying 'Nadanusandhana' as a non-conceptual 'Mukhya-upaya' (primary technique) that bypasses the need for 'Tattva-bodha' (intellectual realization).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This approach aligns with contemporary psychological mindfulness, suggesting that sensory-based grounding techniques (like sound focus) are often more effective for stress reduction and mental clarity than purely theoretical or intellectual exercises.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Laya Yoga and Parampara
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse highlights the vastness of the meditative techniques associated with Laya Yoga, attributed to the primordial Guru, Adinatha (Shiva). It suggests that the path to dissolving the mind into the ultimate reality is infinitely diverse, catering to the varying capacities of practitioners.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It establishes the authority of the lineage (Sampradaya) and emphasizes that spiritual wisdom is not limited to a single rigid method, but encompasses a multitude of pathways to self-realization.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditation on internal sound (Nada), focus on breath, and various sensory withdrawal (Pratyahara) techniques are implied as the 1.25 crore variations of absorption.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Laya refers to the absorption of the chitta (mind-stuff) into the object of meditation or into the pure consciousness (Atman), effectively dissolving the ego-construct.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this validates the 'neuro-diversity' of human consciousness, acknowledging that different individuals require different meditative 'hooks' or anchors to achieve states of deep flow and mental stillness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Raja Yoga and Nadanusandhana
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse emphasizes the physical and energetic preparation required for deep meditation. By assuming a stable posture and the Shambhavi Mudra, the practitioner aligns the internal flow of energy to listen to the divine internal sound (nada).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the synthesis of posture, gesture, and sensory withdrawal, providing a framework for modern practitioners to achieve psychological stability and internal silence.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practices prescribed are: Muktasana (posture), Shambhavi Mudra (gaze technique), and Nadanusandhana (auditory concentration on inner sound).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around Nadanusandhana, the yogic practice of focusing consciousness on the 'Anahata Nada' or primordial sound, which serves as a ladder to reach the Brahmanadi.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: It is highly relevant for cognitive and sensory training; it advocates for 'auditory mindfulness' as a tool for reducing anxiety and achieving deep mental stillness in a noisy, distracted digital age.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
षण्मुखीमुद्रया नादानुसन्धानमाह - श्रवणेति । श्रवणपुटे नयनयोः नेत्रयोः युगलं युग्मं घ्राणशब्देन घ्राणपुटे मुखमास्यम् । एषां द्वन्द्वे प्राण्यङ्गत्वात् एकवद्भावे प्राप्तेऽपि सर्वस्यापि द्वन्द्वैकवद्भावस्य वैकल्पिकत्वात् न भवति । तेषां निरोधनं कराङ्गुलिभिः कार्यम् । निरोधनं चेत्थं -
अङ्गुष्ठाभ्यामुभौ कर्णौ तर्जनीभ्यां च चक्षुषी ।
चकारात् तदन्याभ्यां मुखं प्रच्छाद्य इति समुच्चीयते । शुद्धा प्राणायामैः मलरहिता या सुषुम्नासरणिः सुषुम्नापद्धतिः तस्याममलो नादः स्फुटं व्यक्तं श्रूयते ॥ ६८ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Regarding the method of 'Shanmukhi Mudra' for the exploration of the inner sound (Nada), the text states 'Shravana...'. Shravana-puta (ear-cavities), Nayana-yugala (pair of eyes), Ghrana (nose), and Mukha (mouth). Though a collective singular might be expected in this compound due to the nature of body parts, it is not mandatory. Their restraint is to be done using the fingers of the hands. The method of restraint is as follows: 'Using the two thumbs, close the ears; with the two index fingers, the eyes; and by the others (middle and ring fingers), the mouth.' When the Sushumna canal is purified of all impurities (malas) through Pranayama, the stainless/pure inner sound (Nada) is heard clearly.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: षण्मुखी मुद्रा के माध्यम से नादानुसन्धान की विधि बताई गई है - 'श्रवणपुटादि' का अर्थ है कानों के छिद्र, नेत्रों का युगल, घ्राण (नासिका), और मुख। यद्यपि शरीर के अंगों के द्वन्द्व समास में एकवद्भाव की संभावना है, किंतु विकल्प के कारण ऐसा नहीं हुआ है। इन इंद्रियों का निरोध हाथों की उंगलियों से किया जाना चाहिए। निरोध की विधि यह है - दोनों अंगूठों से कानों को, तर्जनी उंगलियों से नेत्रों को, और शेष उंगलियों से मुख को बंद करें। जब प्राणायाम द्वारा सुषुम्ना नाड़ी मल-रहित शुद्ध हो जाती है, तो उस शुद्ध मार्ग में नाद स्पष्ट रूप से सुनाई देता है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pratyahara (Sensory Withdrawal)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the physical mechanics of Pratyahara as a prerequisite for meditation. By intentionally blocking the sensory inputs of the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth, the practitioner halts the flow of external stimuli to facilitate internal focus.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the physiological discipline required for higher meditative states. In the modern context, it underscores the necessity of managing sensory overload to achieve mental clarity and emotional regulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice is Shanmukhi Mudra: using thumbs for ears, index fingers for eyes, and other fingers for the nose and mouth (or mouth), combined with Pranayama for channel purification.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on Shanmukhi Mudra, where the senses are retracted to achieve Pratyahara. This leads to the purification of the Sushumna-nadi, enabling the aspirant to perceive the Anahata-nada (the unstruck internal sound).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents 'sensory deprivation' to lower cognitive load and achieve deep meditative states (flow state). It is a practical tool to decouple the mind from constant external stimulation and digital distraction.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Nada Yoga (Yoga of Sound)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse introduces the progressive stages of inner sound meditation (Nada-anusandhana). These states represent the evolution of the yogi's consciousness as they withdraw from external sensory stimuli and merge into the subtle internal cosmic sound.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes a structured psychological progression in meditation, suggesting that enlightenment is not instantaneous but a methodical deepening of sensory refinement.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Nada-anusandhana, pratyahara, dhyana, and continuous inward focus on the inner resonance.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is Nada-avastha, describing the developmental phases of dhyana where the practitioner transitions through the stages of Arambha (initiation), Ghata (unification), and Paricaya (stabilization).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a psychological sense, these stages correspond to the process of cognitive decompression and deep focus, which is essential for managing sensory overload and achieving neurobiological coherence in modern life.

commentary_faqs.answer: This term refers to the nascent phase of spiritual discipline where the seeker first commits to the path of Yoga or meditation. It marks the transition from intellectual interest to experiential engagement with the initial steps of practice.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern life, this signifies the necessity of 'getting started' and the discipline required to establish a routine in any transformative pursuit, whether it be meditation, learning, or professional mastery.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Initial steadying of the citta, commencement of abhyasa (sustained practice), and foundational discipline.
commentary_faqs.answer: Arambha-avastha represents the 'prathama bhumi' or initial ground of Yoga where the practitioner begins to focus on the 'dharana' or steadying of the mind.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to the 'activation phase' of behavior modification, crucial for habit formation and overcoming the inertia of stagnation.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Siddhi and Spiritual Transformation
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the state of a practitioner who has attained perfection in Samadhi, leading to a transmutation of the physical form. It suggests that spiritual evolution fundamentally alters the constitution of the individual, shifting from material limitations to transcendental characteristics.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These attributes are often cited in Yoga literature (e.g., Patanjali Yoga Sutra, Shvetashvatara Upanishad) as symptoms of the purification of the elements, representing the harmony between spirit and matter.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditation on the inner light (Jyoti-dhyana), Prana-samyama, and intense Samadhi-abhyasa.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'Kaya-siddhi' (perfection of the body), where the 'Pancha-bhuta' (five elements) are purified, leading to 'divyata' (divinity) within the physical structure.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the state of psychosomatic integration where deep mental clarity and the release of chronic stress lead to optimal biological vitality and radiant health.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Yoga Philosophy (Ghata Avastha)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse outlines the foundational elements of the Ghata Avastha (the 'pot' or 'vessel' state), which is the first of the four stages of Yoga practice in Hatha Yoga. It emphasizes the integration of physical life-forces (Prana-Apana) with transcendental sound and consciousness, leading to the identification of the individual with the Universal.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It remains highly relevant as a meditative framework for internalizing attention, moving from physiological breath control to the realization of metaphysical non-duality.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama (breath regulation), Nada-anusandhana (concentration on inner sound), and Dhyana (meditation on the Bindu).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is the unification of 'prāṇa-apāna' and 'jīva-ātman' with 'param-ātman', signifying the 'ghata-avasthā' where the body acts as a vessel for divine union.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Provides a psychological framework for stress reduction by transitioning from external sensory preoccupation to internal awareness, fostering emotional and spiritual stability.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes a stage in meditative absorption (Samadhi) where the practitioner transcends the emotional and identity-based obstacles represented by the Vishnu-granthi. Once this energetic knot is pierced, the consciousness is liberated into a state of uninterrupted divine joy.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient understanding of neuro-energetic centers within the human body, serving as a roadmap for practitioners of meditative paths to track internal spiritual progress.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Meditation (Dhyana), Breath control (Pranayama), and Kundalini awakening techniques.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept refers to the 'Granthi-bheda' (breaking of the knots), specifically the 'Vishnu-granthi', which signifies the dissolution of the ego-attachment to the heart's emotional experiences, leading to the experience of 'Paramananda' (Supreme Bliss).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern psychological context, this relates to the 'unblocking' of deep-seated emotional traumas and restrictive habit patterns, allowing for a state of mental equanimity and increased subjective well-being.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Nada Yoga (Yoga of Sound)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the third stage of an internal auditory experience, wherein the practitioner perceives the resonance of a Mardala drum within the subtle space (Akasha) of consciousness. It signifies the intensification of concentration as the practitioner progresses through various stages of internal sound perception.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This is central to the practice of Laya Yoga and Nada Yoga, emphasizing that sensory withdrawal leads to the perception of transcendental sound vibrations, which are considered subtle markers of spiritual progress.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses), Dhyana (meditation), and Nada-anusamdhana (the tracking and fixation on internal sound currents).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Parichaya-avastha', the third stage of Nada-yoga where internal sounds undergo a specific modulation characteristic of the progression toward absorption.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: From a psychological perspective, this represents the transition from external focus to internal sensory monitoring, facilitating a state of deep mindfulness and auditory hypersensitivity, which can lead to stress reduction and altered states of consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Sahajananda (Innate Bliss)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse differentiates between the transitory joy experienced by the fluctuating mind (citta) and the eternal, unconditioned joy (sahaja) that emerges when mental modifications are transcended. By mastering the mind, the practitioner uncovers the substrate of pure consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This aligns with the yogic and Vedantic emphasis on moving beyond 'manas' (sensory mind) to 'atman' (self), remaining highly relevant in modern psychology as a technique for emotional regulation and mindfulness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Jitwa (Conquering the mental fluctuations/vritis) and Samadhi (the state of absorption in innate bliss).
commentary_faqs.answer: The transition from vikalpa-based cittananda to the niralamba sahajananda, representing the shift from object-dependent joy to the swarupa-avasthana of the self.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Provides a psychological framework for distinguishing between dopamine-driven, transitory satisfaction and the deep, sustainable state of contentment often sought in cognitive-behavioral wellness models.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
नानाविधं नादमाह द्वाभ्याम् - आदौ इति । आदौ वायोः ब्रह्मरन्ध्रगमनसमये जलधिः समुद्रः जीमूतः मेघो भेरी वाद्यविशेषः ‘भेरी स्त्री दुन्दुभिः पुमान्’ इत्यमरः (१.८.६) । झर्झरो वाद्यविशेषः ।
‘वाद्यप्रभेदा डमरुमड्डु डिण्डिमझर्झराः ।
मर्दलः पणवोऽन्येपि --’ इत्यमरः (१.८.८)
जलधिप्रमुखेभ्यः सम्भव इव सम्भवो येषां ते तथा मध्ये ब्रह्मरन्ध्रे वायोः स्थैर्यानन्तरं मर्दलो वाद्यविशेषः शङ्खो जलजः ताभ्यामुत्था इव मर्दलशङ्खोत्थाः । घण्टाकाहलौ वाद्यविशेषौ ताभ्यां जाता इव घण्टाकाहलजाः ॥ ८५ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: जाग्रत्स्वप्नसुषुप्तिमूर्च्छामरणलक्षणाः पञ्च व्युत्थानावस्थाः ताभिः विशेषेण मुक्तो रहितः सर्वाः याः चिन्ताः स्मृतयः ताभिः विवर्जितः विरहितो यो योगः सकलवृत्तिनिरोधः अस्यास्तीति योगी तुर्यावस्थावान् स मुक्तो जीवन्नेव मुक्तः । सकलवृत्तिनिरोधे आत्मनः स्वरूपावस्थानात् । तदुक्तं पातञ्जले सूत्रे ‘तदा द्रष्टुः स्वरूपे अवस्थानम्’ (१.३) इति । स्पष्टमन्यत् ॥ १०७ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
‘आलस्यं प्रथमो विघ्नो द्वितीयस्तु प्रकथ्यते ।
मार्कण्डेय पुराणे (४०.१-६) -
‘उपसर्गाः प्रवर्तन्ते दृष्टा ह्यात्मनि योगिनः ।
काम्याः क्रियास्तथा कामान् मनुष्यो योऽभिवाञ्छति ।
देवत्वममरेशत्वं रसायनचयः क्रियाः ।
श्राद्धानां सर्वदानानां फलानि नियमांस्तथा ।
तेभ्यस्तेभ्यश्च कर्मभ्यः उपसृष्टोऽभिवाञ्छति ।
चित्तमित्थं वर्तमानं यत्नाद् योगी निवर्तयेत् ।
ब्रह्मसङ्गि मनः कुर्वन् उपसर्गात् प्रमुच्यते । ’ इति ।
स्कन्दपुराणे -
‘यदैभिरन्तरायैर्न क्षिप्यतेऽस्य हि मानसम् ।
योगभस्करे -
‘सात्विकीं धृतिमालम्ब्य योगी सत्त्वेन सुस्थिरः ।
एवं योगमुपासीनः शक्रदिपदनिस्पृहः ।
‘विस्तरस्य भिया नोक्ताः सन्ति विघ्नाः ह्यनेकशः ।
